title: Learn AWS from the infrastructure up
hook: Amazon Web Services (AWS) is a cloud platform where you rent compute, storage, and networking instead of buying servers. This track starts with how Regions, Availability Zones, and Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) actually work behind the scenes, then deepens into the services you already use — S3, Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, CloudWatch, and DataSync — with interview-ready depth.

blocks.text: AWS is Amazon's cloud platform: a global collection of data centers organized into Regions and Availability Zones (AZs). You create resources — Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs), Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances, Simple Storage Service (S3) buckets, Lambda functions — through a control plane API. AWS provisions and manages the physical infrastructure; you configure networking, security, and application logic. The shared responsibility model means AWS secures the cloud; you secure what you put in it.

entries.plainDefinition: A geographic area containing multiple isolated Availability Zones. Data and resources stay within the Region unless you explicitly replicate.
entries.example: us-east-1 (N. Virginia) is one Region; ap-south-1 (Mumbai) is another.

entries.plainDefinition: One or more discrete data centers within a Region, with independent power and networking. Deploy across multiple AZs for high availability.
entries.example: An Auto Scaling Group spanning us-east-1a and us-east-1b survives a single-AZ failure.

entries.plainDefinition: Your isolated network inside AWS. You define IP ranges, subnets, route tables, and gateways.
entries.example: A three-tier app often uses public subnets for load balancers and private subnets for databases.

entries.plainDefinition: A distributed cache at edge locations that serves content closer to users. AWS CloudFront is the CDN service.
entries.example: Static assets from S3 are cached at edge locations worldwide.

blocks.text: In a datacenter you buy servers, rack them, cable switches, and manage power. In AWS you define intent — a VPC, an Auto Scaling Group, an SQS queue — and the control plane provisions capacity. Networking is software-defined: route tables replace physical routers, security groups replace rack firewalls, and NAT Gateways replace edge routers. Multi-tenancy is built in: your VPC is isolated from other customers at the hypervisor and network layer.

blocks.text: Modules are numbered in learning order. If you already use SQS and Lambda but VPC feels fuzzy, still read modules 01–07 before jumping to service internals — packet flow and tenancy boundaries explain most production bugs.

items.title: Foundations (modules 01–07)
items.body: Cloud mental model, global infrastructure, accounts and IAM, networking primer, VPC, connectivity, and perimeter security. Finish before deep-diving Lambda in VPC.

items.title: Intermediate (modules 08–13)
items.body: CloudFront, EC2, S3, Lambda, SQS, Step Functions — services you ship weekly, explained behind the scenes.

items.title: Advanced (modules 14–18)
items.body: CloudWatch runbooks, DataSync, Well-Architected pillars, landing zones, and SaaS multi-tenancy.

items.title: Revise with mind maps and interview pages
items.body: Use mind maps and interview sections after topic pages — not as a shortcut around fundamentals.

items.title: Senior / FAANG depth layer (5+ years)
items.body: On intermediate and advanced topics (08–18), read Senior interview depth after beginner sections. Priority: VPC packet tracing (05–07), Lambda in VPC (11), SQS idempotency (12), Well-Architected tradeoffs (16), SaaS tenancy (18).

sections.heading: What you'll build along the way

blocks.text: Every topic uses AWS CLI commands and CloudFormation YAML — not console screenshots. Examples mirror real backend shapes: SQS consumers, Lambda in VPC, Step Functions sagas, CloudFront + S3 static sites, DataSync migrations, and multi-tenant SaaS routing. C# and Node backend correlations appear wherever they help you transfer what you already know.

blocks.title: 98 topics — beginner clarity plus senior depth
blocks.body: Every topic keeps plain-English hooks and glossaries. Intermediate and advanced modules add control-plane internals, VPC Flow Logs, and FAANG-style interview scripts without removing the beginner layer.
